files.samples/iyi/app/greeter.iyi: # A module other files can import. See `../modules.iyi`. # # R-1: the module path is the compilation unit's name, and it is absolute — # resolved from the project root, never relative to whoever imports it. That # is what makes `app/greeter` mean the same module in every file that writes # it. The file lives at `app/greeter.iyi` because the path says so. module app/greeter pub trait Greet abstract def greet : String end pub def polite(name : String) : String "#{greeting}, #{name}." end # R-2: not exported, so this is the module's own business. `modules.iyi` can # neither `using app/greeter::{greeting}` nor reach it by any other route — # `.iyimod` carries a module's exports and nothing else, so a name left # unmarked has to be unreachable or that metadata would not be enough to # compile against (SPEC.md IV.2). def greeting : String "Hello" end # Also exported, and deliberately named the same as something in # `app/formal` — see how `modules.iyi` has to deal with that. pub def title : String "friend" end
files.samples/iyi/basics.iyi: # The first half hour — what a person writes before they write anything real. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/basics.iyi # # The other samples each document a rule. This one documents nothing: it is # here because the prelude grows only when a program in this repository needs # something (SPEC.md 0.1.0 item 3), and a person meeting the language writes # these six programs before they write a module. Every method this file calls # is one somebody reached for in their first half hour and did not find. module samples/basics # 1. Counting, with a range rather than a `while`. total = 0 (1..10).each { |i| total = total + i } puts total # => 55 # 2. FizzBuzz, because it is the first thing anybody types. (1..15).each do |i| if i % 15 == 0 puts "FizzBuzz" elsif i % 3 == 0 puts "Fizz" elsif i % 5 == 0 puts "Buzz" else puts i end end # 3. Picking things out of a list. numbers = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6] puts numbers.first # => 3 puts numbers.select { |n| n > 3 }.join(",") # => 4,5,9,6 puts numbers.includes?(9) # => true puts numbers.sorted.join(",") # => 1,1,2,3,4,5,6,9 puts numbers.join(",") # => 3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6, untouched # The pair. `sorted` hands back a copy and `sort_in_place` changes the array, # and the second one is spelled out on purpose: Crystal calls the copy `sort` # and the mutating one `sort!`, a name that cannot be written here, so a plain # `sort` would mean one thing in this library and the opposite in Crystal's # (SPEC.md III.1.7a). numbers.sort_in_place { |a, b| a < b ? -1 : (a == b ? 0 : 1) } puts numbers.join(",") # => 1,1,2,3,4,5,6,9 # 4. Adding them up two ways. puts numbers.sum # => 31 puts numbers.reduce(0) { |a, b| a + b } # => 31 # 5. Text. greeting = "Hello, World" puts greeting.downcase # => hello, world puts greeting.includes?("World") # => true puts greeting.size # => 12 # 6. Counting words, which is where a dictionary earns its place. counts = {} of String => Int32 ["a", "b", "a", "c", "a"].each do |word| counts[word] = (counts[word]? || 0) + 1 end puts counts["a"] # => 3 puts counts.size # => 3

files.samples/iyi/calc/ast.iyi: module calc/ast # What an evaluated program can go wrong with. Both are ordinary members of the # union an evaluation returns (SPEC.md III.1), so a caller either handles them # or propagates with `!`. pub struct UnknownName getter name : String def initialize(@name : String) end end impl Error for UnknownName def message : String "unknown name '#{name}'" end end pub struct DividedByZero def initialize end end impl Error for DividedByZero def message : String "divided by zero" end end # The one thing every node can do. A trait rather than a base class, because # there is nothing to inherit and R-3 has no opinion to break here. pub trait Node abstract def evaluate(scope : Hash(String, Int32)) : Int32 | UnknownName | DividedByZero end pub struct Number getter value : Int32 def initialize(@value : Int32) end end impl Node for Number def evaluate(scope : Hash(String, Int32)) : Int32 | UnknownName | DividedByZero value end end pub struct Name getter name : String def initialize(@name : String) end end impl Node for Name def evaluate(scope : Hash(String, Int32)) : Int32 | UnknownName | DividedByZero return UnknownName.new(name) unless scope.has_key?(name) scope[name] end end pub class Binary getter op : Char getter left : Number | Name | Binary getter right : Number | Name | Binary def initialize(@op : Char, @left : Number | Name | Binary, @right : Number | Name | Binary) end end impl Node for Binary def evaluate(scope : Hash(String, Int32)) : Int32 | UnknownName | DividedByZero a = left.evaluate(scope)! b = right.evaluate(scope)! if op == '+' a + b elsif op == '-' a - b elsif op == '*' a * b else return DividedByZero.new if b == 0 a // b end end end
files.samples/iyi/calc/lexer.iyi: module calc/lexer # What the scanner produces. A token is its kind, the text it covers and where # it started, because an error that cannot say where is half an error. pub struct Token getter kind : String getter text : String getter at : Int32 def initialize(@kind : String, @text : String, @at : Int32) end end pub struct BadCharacter getter at : Int32 getter found : Char def initialize(@at : Int32, @found : Char) end end impl Error for BadCharacter def message : String "unexpected character at #{at}" end end pub def scan(source : String) : Array(Token) | BadCharacter tokens = [] of Token index = 0 while index < source.size c = source[index] if c == ' ' || c == '\n' || c == '\t' index = index + 1 elsif digit?(c) start = index while index < source.size && digit?(source[index]) index = index + 1 end tokens << Token.new("number", source[start, index - start], start) elsif letter?(c) start = index while index < source.size && (letter?(source[index]) || digit?(source[index])) index = index + 1 end tokens << Token.new("name", source[start, index - start], start) elsif operator?(c) tokens << Token.new("op", source[index, 1], index) index = index + 1 else return BadCharacter.new(index, c) end end tokens << Token.new("end", "", index) tokens end def digit?(c : Char) : Bool c >= '0' && c <= '9' end def letter?(c : Char) : Bool (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') || (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') || c == '_' end def operator?(c : Char) : Bool c == '+' || c == '-' || c == '*' || c == '/' || c == '(' || c == ')' || c == '=' end
files.samples/iyi/calc/parser.iyi: module calc/parser import calc/lexer import calc/ast using calc/lexer::{Token} using calc/ast::{Number, Name, Binary} pub struct SyntaxError getter at : Int32 getter wanted : String def initialize(@at : Int32, @wanted : String) end end impl Error for SyntaxError def message : String "expected #{wanted} at #{at}" end end # One statement: `name = expression`, or an expression on its own, which the # runner prints. Kept as a pair rather than a node type, because a statement is # not something this language evaluates twice. pub struct Statement getter target : String getter body : Number | Name | Binary def initialize(@target : String, @body : Number | Name | Binary) end end # A cursor over the tokens. A struct with an index rather than a shifting array, # because backing up one token is the parser's whole trick. pub class Reader getter tokens : Array(Token) getter at : Int32 def initialize(@tokens : Array(Token)) @at = 0 end def peek : Token tokens[at] end def advance : Token token = tokens[at] @at = at + 1 token end end pub def parse(tokens : Array(Token)) : Array(Statement) | SyntaxError reader = Reader.new(tokens) statements = [] of Statement while reader.peek.kind != "end" statements << statement(reader)! end statements end def statement(reader : Reader) : Statement | SyntaxError first = reader.peek if first.kind == "name" && reader.tokens[reader.at + 1].text == "=" reader.advance reader.advance Statement.new(first.text, expression(reader)!) else Statement.new("", expression(reader)!) end end def expression(reader : Reader) : Number | Name | Binary | SyntaxError left = term(reader)! while reader.peek.kind == "op" && (reader.peek.text == "+" || reader.peek.text == "-") op = reader.advance.text[0] left = Binary.new(op, left, term(reader)!) end left end def term(reader : Reader) : Number | Name | Binary | SyntaxError left = factor(reader)! while reader.peek.kind == "op" && (reader.peek.text == "*" || reader.peek.text == "/") op = reader.advance.text[0] left = Binary.new(op, left, factor(reader)!) end left end def factor(reader : Reader) : Number | Name | Binary | SyntaxError token = reader.advance if token.kind == "number" Number.new(token.text.to_i) elsif token.kind == "name" Name.new(token.text) elsif token.text == "(" inside = expression(reader)! closing = reader.advance return SyntaxError.new(closing.at, "')'") unless closing.text == ")" inside else SyntaxError.new(token.at, "a number, a name or '('") end end
files.samples/iyi/calc.iyi: # A language, in the language — the biggest program this prelude can hold. # # echo "x = 2 + 3 * 4 # x * 10" | ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/calc.iyi # # The other samples each document a rule. This one documents nothing and is # here for a different reason: everything else in `samples/iyi` is a page long, # and a language that has only been used for pages has not been used. This is # three modules and a scanner, a parser and an evaluator, the shape of every # real program that reads something, written against iyi's own 5,674-line # library and nothing else. # # What it cost to write is recorded where it landed. `String#[]`, `String#[](start, # count)`, `String#to_i` and `read_input` are in the prelude because this file # asked for them, which is the rule the prelude grows by (SPEC.md "0.1.0", # item 3). Nothing else was missing. module samples/calc import calc/lexer import calc/parser import calc/ast using calc/lexer::{scan, BadCharacter} using calc/parser::{parse, Statement, SyntaxError} using calc/ast::{Number, Name, Binary, UnknownName, DividedByZero} # What runs when nothing is piped in, so that the sample is a program rather # than a prompt. CI runs it this way. DEMO = "x = 2 + 3 * 4 y = (x - 4) / 2 x + y * 10 missing + 1 1 / 0" pub def run(source : String) : Nil tokens = scan(source) if tokens.is_a?(BadCharacter) puts "error: #{tokens.message}" return end program = parse(tokens) if program.is_a?(SyntaxError) puts "error: #{program.message}" return end scope = {} of String => Int32 program.each do |statement| value = statement.body.evaluate(scope) if value.is_a?(Int32) if statement.target.empty? puts value else scope[statement.target] = value end else # `value` is an error member of the union, and every one of them answers # `message` because they implement `Error` (SPEC.md III.1). puts "error: #{value.message}" end end end typed = read_input run(typed.empty? ? DEMO : typed)
files.samples/iyi/collections.iyi: # The `Enumerable` port, exercised — SPEC.md II.6. # # ./bin/crystal run samples/iyi/collections.iyi # # `std/enumerable.iyi` holds the trait. This file implements it twice and calls # every method it defines. Both matter: a default method is only typed when it # is called, so a trait that merely compiles has proved nothing about whether # its bodies are sound. # # `Nums` and `Words` answer `Elem` differently — `Int32` and `String` — and each # gets the same 57 default methods from one `each`. That is the claim II.6 # makes, running. module samples/collections import std/enumerable using std/enumerable::{Enumerable} pub struct Nums def initialize(@a : Array(Int32)) end end impl Enumerable for Nums type Elem = Int32 def each(& : Int32 -> Nil) : Nil @a.each { |x| yield x } end end pub struct Words def initialize(@a : Array(String)) end end impl Enumerable for Words type Elem = String def each(& : String -> Nil) : Nil @a.each { |x| yield x } end end n = Nums.new([3, 1, 4, 1, 5]) w = Words.new(["pear", "fig", "plum", "kiwi"]) puts "to_a #{n.to_a.join(",")}" puts "size #{n.size}" puts "empty? #{n.empty?} #{Nums.new([] of Int32).empty?}" puts "all? #{n.all? { |x| x > 0 }}" puts "any? #{n.any? { |x| x > 4 }}" puts "none? #{n.none? { |x| x > 9 }}" puts "one? #{n.one? { |x| x == 4 }}" puts "count #{n.count { |x| x == 1 }}" puts "find? #{n.find? { |x| x > 3 }} #{n.find? { |x| x > 9 }.inspect}" puts "find #{n.find { |x| x > 3 }}" puts "index? #{n.index? { |x| x == 4 }}" puts "index #{n.index { |x| x == 4 }}" puts "first?/first #{n.first?} #{n.first}" puts "map #{n.map { |x| x * 2 }.join(",")}" puts "flat_map #{n.flat_map { |x| [x, x] }.join(",")}" puts "map_with_index #{n.map_with_index { |x, i| x * i }.join(",")}" puts "select #{n.select { |x| x > 2 }.join(",")}" puts "reject #{n.reject { |x| x > 2 }.join(",")}" puts "partition #{n.partition { |x| x > 2 }.map(&.join("+")).join(" | ")}" puts "take/skip #{n.take(2).join(",")} #{n.skip(3).join(",")}" puts "take_while #{n.take_while { |x| x < 4 }.join(",")}" puts "skip_while #{n.skip_while { |x| x < 4 }.join(",")}" puts "reduce #{n.reduce(0) { |a, x| a + x }}" puts "each_with_index #{n.map_with_index { |x, i| i }.join(",")}" puts "each_with_object #{n.each_with_object([] of Int32) { |o, e| o << e * 10 }.join(",")}" puts "join #{n.join("-")}" puts "includes? #{n.includes?(4)} #{n.includes?(9)}" puts "max?/max #{n.max?} #{n.max}" puts "min?/min #{n.min?} #{n.min}" puts "sum/product #{n.sum} #{n.product}" puts "sum of nothing #{Nums.new([] of Int32).sum}" puts "tally #{n.tally[1]}" puts "sorted #{n.sorted.join(",")}" puts "max_by #{w.max_by { |s| s.size }}" puts "group_by #{w.group_by { |s| s.size }[4].join(",")}" puts "index_by #{w.index_by { |s| s.size }[3]}" puts "each_slice #{n.each_slice(2).map(&.join("+")).join(" ")}" puts "each_cons #{n.each_cons(2).map(&.join("+")).join(" ")}" puts "chunk_while #{n.chunk_while { |a, b| b >= a }.map(&.join("+")).join(" ")}" puts "first(n) #{n.first(3).join(",")}" puts "compact_map #{n.compact_map { |x| x > 2 ? x * 10 : nil }.join(",")}" puts "find_value #{n.find_value { |x| x > 3 ? "big" : nil }}" puts "accumulate #{n.accumulate(0) { |a, x| a + x }.join(",")}" puts "reduce? #{n.reduce? { |a, x| a + x }}" puts "in_groups_of #{n.in_groups_of(2, 0).map(&.join("+")).join(" ")}" puts "min_by #{w.min_by { |s| s.size }}" puts "max_of/min_of #{w.max_of { |s| s.size }} #{w.min_of { |s| s.size }}" puts "minmax #{n.minmax[0]},#{n.minmax[1]}" puts "tally_by #{w.tally_by { |s| s.size }[4]}" puts "sum_by #{w.sum_by { |s| s.size }}" # SPEC II.6 finding 6: one bound replaces `Indexable | Iterable | Iterator`, # and `O::Elem` names what the other collection yields. puts "zip #{n.zip(w).map { |pair| "#{pair[0]}#{pair[1]}" }.join(" ")}" cycled = [] of Int32 Nums.new([1, 2]).cycle(2) { |x| cycled << x } puts "cycle #{cycled.join(",")}" # A trait with an associated type used as a type: one function, any implementer. def describe(e : Enumerable) : String "#{e.size} items" end puts "as a type #{describe(n)} / #{describe(w)}" # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # What this sample would report as an error # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * `Words.new([...]).sum` — `sum` is bounded `where Elem : Num` and # `String` implements `Cmp` but not `Num`. The error names the element type # and the bound rather than failing somewhere inside the method body. # # * A second `impl Enumerable for Nums` — a trait with an associated type is # implementable once per type, because a second answer for `Elem` would make # every call on `Nums` ambiguous. # # * `impl Num for X` with no `impl Cmp for X` before it — `Num : Cmp` requires # it, and the impls have to be written in dependency order.
files.samples/iyi/derive.iyi: # `derive`, and where it runs (SPEC.md R-5, II.4). # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/derive.iyi # # A derive runs once, in the module that declares the type. What it generates is # an ordinary declaration of that module, so it travels in the module's # `.iyimod` and a consumer calls the derived method without running the macro # and without this module's source. `bench/samples_roundtrip.sh` builds this # sample from its artifacts with `std/derives` deleted, which is that claim # taken literally. # # The macro is handed the facts R-5 lets it read: the declaration's name, and # the fields written in its body, each with the type it was written as. It # cannot enumerate a type it was not given, which is what keeps a derive # bounded and cacheable. module samples/derive import std/derives using std/derives pub struct Point @x : Int32 @y : Int32 def initialize(@x : Int32, @y : Int32) end derive described end # One derive, two declarations. The macro reads each one's own fields, so # neither type had to be written down inside the macro. pub struct Span @from : Int32 @to : Int32 @label : String def initialize(@from : Int32, @to : Int32, @label : String) end derive described end puts Point.new(3, 4).described puts Span.new(1, 9, "range").described # The field type is a type, not a name, so a derive can ask what it implements. # `Name` and `Show` both belong to `std/derives`, and both arrive from that # module's artifact when its source is gone: `@label` is rendered through the # trait, and `@count` is skipped because `Int32` does not implement it. # # `getter label : Name` is a macro call, so the field it declares exists only # once it has run. A derive reads the declarations above it, which is why # `derive` goes last. Below `getter`, this would be an error rather than a # method generated over no fields. # # One line, two derives: each macro reads the same declaration and adds its own # methods. pub struct Tag getter label : Name @count : Int32 def initialize(@label : Name, @count : Int32) end derive described, shown end puts Tag.new(Name.new("hi"), 2).described puts Tag.new(Name.new("hi"), 2).shown # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # What this sample would report as an error # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * `derive missing` where nothing exports a `missing` macro. The error names # the macro and the declaration it would have to be written as, rather than # failing as an undefined method on the type's metaclass. # # * `derive` outside a class or struct body. There is no declaration to read, # so there is nothing for the macro to be handed. # # * A `derive` inside a reopened type from another module. That is refused # before the derive is reached, by R-3: iyi has no open classes, so a module # cannot add to a type it does not declare. # # * A `getter` (or any macro call that declares a field) written below the # `derive` that should read it. The derive names the call and says which way # to move, rather than generating a method over the fields it happened to see.
files.samples/iyi/errors.iyi: # Errors are ordinary union members — SPEC.md III.1. # # ./bin/crystal run samples/iyi/errors.iyi # # No `Result` wrapper, no exception hierarchy, no new type machinery: unions # already exist and already carry a type id. What makes a member an *error* # member is that its type implements `Error`, a trait the compiler owns. module samples/errors pub struct IOError getter path : String def initialize(@path : String) end end # `Error` is not declared here. It is the compiler's, so that `!` can ask # whether a member implements it without a name in scope deciding the answer. impl Error for IOError def message : String "no such file: #{path}" end end pub struct ParseError getter text : String def initialize(@text : String) end end impl Error for ParseError def message : String "not a number: #{text}" end end pub def read(path : String) : String | IOError return IOError.new(path) if path == "missing" path == "bad" ? "twelve" : "12" end pub def to_number(text : String) : Int32 | ParseError return ParseError.new(text) unless text == "12" 12 end # `!` propagates. If the value is a non-error member the expression evaluates to # it — narrowed, so `to_number` sees a `String` and not the union. If it is an # error member it is returned from here, which is why `load` has to admit both # errors in its own return type. Nothing enforces that separately: it is the # ordinary return-type check on the return the operator writes. pub def load(path : String) : Int32 | IOError | ParseError text = read(path)! to_number(text)! end # Handling needs nothing new. An exhaustive `case` already checks totality, so # adding an error member to `load` turns every incomplete `case` on it into a # compile error. That is the main ergonomic argument for the whole approach and # it cost nothing to build. ["config", "missing", "bad"].each do |path| case load(path) in Int32 then puts "read #{it}" in IOError then puts "io: #{it.message}" in ParseError then puts "parse: #{it.message}" end end # `it` is the value being matched, and it is narrowed per branch: the first sees # an `Int32`, the other two see one error type each, which is how `.message` # resolves without anything asking what the union holds. It is an assignment the # compiler writes into each branch, not new machinery — so `it` outlives the # `case` the way any variable assigned inside an `if` does, and a nested `case` # shadows it. # Where a `case` is overkill, `.or` takes a default and `.or_panic` takes the # value or dies (III.1.3). These cannot be ordinary methods: by II.1 a real # method call on `Int32 | IOError` would demand it from *both* members, and a # method every error type has to supply is what this design avoids. So the # compiler knows them by name — which is also why `or` and `or_panic` are not # names an iyi program can use for anything else. ["config", "missing", "bad"].each do |path| puts "or: #{load(path).or(0)}" end # `.or` is an `is_a?(::Error)` and nothing more, so the result type falls out # instead of being computed: the default's type unioned with the non-error # members. Here that is `Int32`, and the default is only evaluated when there is # an error to recover from. puts "or: #{load("missing").or(-1)}" # `.or_panic` yields the non-error members alone, because what it calls never # returns. It reaches `message` on a value narrowed to `IOError | ParseError` — # two unrelated types — which resolves by II.1: both implement `Error`, so their # union does. Until panics exist (III.1.4), this unwinds as a Crystal exception. puts "panic: #{load("config").or_panic}" # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # defer — III.1.4 # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # Once errors are values returned early, the interesting exit from a body is an # ordinary `return` in the middle of it, and `begin`/`ensure` makes you wrap # everything after the acquisition to cover it. `defer` names the cleanup at the # acquisition instead. It expands to that same `ensure`, so it runs on a normal # exit, on a `!` propagation, and on an unwind — no new runtime machinery, only # a different shape. pub def session(path : String) : Int32 | IOError | ParseError puts " open outer" defer puts " close outer" text = read(path)! puts " open inner" defer puts " close inner" to_number(text)! end # Cleanup is LIFO, and that is the nesting rather than a rule: the second # `defer` expands inside the first one's body, so its `ensure` is the inner one. # The failing run proves the part that matters — `read(path)!` returns from the # middle of the body and the cleanup still happens. puts "success:" puts session("config").or(-1) puts "propagating:" puts session("missing").or(-1) # The scope is the block, not the function. This is the departure from Go, and # it is what the expansion does rather than an extra rule: the cleanup lands # inside the loop body, so it runs each iteration instead of piling up until the # function returns — Go's best-known wart with the feature. 2.times do |i| defer puts " iteration #{i} closed" puts " iteration #{i}" end # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # What this sample would report as an error # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * Dropping the `in ParseError` branch — `case is not exhaustive`. # # * `def go : String` with `read(p)!` in it — the error names the return type # and the error being propagated into it. # # * `!` on something with no error member, such as an `Int32?`. Rejected rather # than given a surprising meaning: `Nil` does not implement `Error` (III.1.5), # so without the check this would compile and silently do nothing. # # * `!` on a value whose every member is an error. It could never produce one, # and a function that genuinely never succeeds returns `NoReturn`. # # * `def sort!` — `!` is not part of a name (III.1.7). This is the one place # that still explains the naming convention, because after a `def` name there # is nothing to propagate. # # * `.or` and `.or_panic` on the same two operands `!` rejects. With no error # member there is nothing to recover; with every member an error, `.or` can # only return its default and `.or_panic` can only panic. # # * `.or 0` without parentheses — `.or` takes the default in parentheses, so # the shape cannot be confused with a call to a method of that name. # # * `it` in a `case` over a tuple, such as `case {a, b}` — there is no single # value to name, so `it` stays undefined rather than being bound to one of # the elements. # # * `defer close(f)!` — a `defer` runs while the scope is already being left, # possibly carrying an error of its own, so a second one leaving from there # is the error-during-error problem. Handle it in the `defer` body. # # * `impl Error for String` here — the orphan rule (R-3). `Error` is the # compiler's and `String` is the prelude's, so neither belongs to a module # this impl could be at home in, and every module that can name both would be # free to write its own. # # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Not yet implemented # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * Panics (III.1.4). They are meant to be catchable only at task boundaries, # and what a task boundary is belongs to Part V.5. files.samples/iyi/generics.iyi: # Implementing a trait for a generic type — SPEC.md II.7. # # ./bin/crystal run samples/iyi/generics.iyi module samples/generics pub trait Show abstract def show : String end pub struct Box(T) getter value : T def initialize(@value : T) end end # `forall T` introduces the parameter, and it is required. Without it, whether # `T` names a new parameter or a type already in scope would depend on what # happens to be imported — so a library could change what this impl means by # adding an export. Rust requires the same binder for the same reason. impl Show for Box(T) forall T def show : String "Box(#{value})" end end pub struct Pair(A, B) getter first : A getter second : B def initialize(@first : A, @second : B) end end # `Pair` declared its parameters `A, B`; this impl calls them `X, Y`. The names # are the impl's own and bind positionally, so an impl states arity and not # vocabulary — what a type chose to call its parameters is its own business. # Crystal requires a reopened generic to repeat the declared names; that leaks # the declaration's naming into every impl of it. impl Show for Pair(X, Y) forall X, Y def show : String "#{label(first)}, #{label(second)}" end def label(v : X) : String "first=#{v}" end def label(v : Y) : String "second=#{v}" end end puts Box.new(42).show puts Box.new("hello").show puts Pair.new(1, "two").show # One impl covers every instantiation, so instantiations of the same generic # dispatch through the trait together. shown = [Box.new(1), Box.new("two"), Pair.new(3, "four")] of Show shown.each { |s| puts s.show } # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Associated types — SPEC.md II.6 # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # `type Elem` declares a type the *impl* answers, not one the caller picks. A # collection iterates one way, so its element type is an output of the impl; # making it a parameter would leave a call on the collection ambiguous about # which impl it meant. This is the shape `Enumerable` needs: 130 methods # written against `Elem`, on one `abstract def each`. pub trait Container type Elem abstract def first : Elem # A default method. `Elem` resolves to whatever the impl answered, so this # one body serves every implementer without being written per type. def pair : Array(Elem) [first, first] end end pub struct Names def initialize end end impl Container for Names type Elem = String def first : String "ada" end end pub struct Counts def initialize end end impl Container for Counts type Elem = Int32 def first : Int32 42 end end puts Names.new.pair.join(", ") puts Counts.new.pair.sum # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Bounds and requirements — SPEC.md II.6 # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # About a quarter of `Enumerable` is valid only for some element types: `max` # needs `Comparable`, `sum` needs `Numeric`, `tally` needs `Hashable`. `where` # says so. Crystal duck-types these and fails at instantiation naming neither # the bound nor the element type. pub trait Cmp abstract def cmp(other : self) : Int32 end # `Ord : Cmp` requires an implementer to implement `Cmp` too. A requirement, # not an inclusion: implementing `Ord` does not hand a type `Cmp`'s methods, # it insists the type has its own `impl Cmp for` it. Were it an include, every # implementer of `Ord` would satisfy `Cmp` with no impl anywhere — the open # class hole R-3 exists to close. pub trait Ord : Cmp type Item abstract def item : Item # `Ord` never declares `cmp`; the requirement is what guarantees it is there. def beats(other : self) : Bool cmp(other) > 0 end # Valid only when the item type is comparable. `Ranked` answers `Item` with # `Score`, which implements `Cmp`, so this one is callable there. def best : Item where Item : Cmp item end end pub struct Score getter n : Int32 def initialize(@n : Int32) end end impl Cmp for Score def cmp(other : self) : Int32 n - other.n end end pub struct Ranked getter n : Int32 def initialize(@n : Int32) end end impl Cmp for Ranked def cmp(other : self) : Int32 n - other.n end end impl Ord for Ranked type Item = Score def item : Score Score.new(n) end end puts Ranked.new(2).beats(Ranked.new(1)) puts Ranked.new(7).best.n # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # What this sample would report as an error # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * `impl Ord for X` with no `impl Cmp for X` before it — the error names the # required trait. The impls have to be written in dependency order, because # the check runs where the impl is and nothing has looked ahead. # # * `Ranked.new(1).best` if `Item` were answered with a type that does not # implement `Cmp` — the error names the element type and the bound, which is # the whole reason the bound is written. # # * A second `impl Container for Names` — a trait with associated types is # implementable only once for a type. That restriction *is* the difference # from a parameter: a second answer for `Elem` would make `Names.new.first` # ambiguous. A trait with parameters has no such rule, because several impls # are the point of having parameters. # # * `impl Container for Names` with no `type Elem = ...` — the error names the # associated type left unanswered. # # * `type Elem = String` written in the trait — a trait declares an associated # type, it does not answer it. # # * `impl Show for Box(T)` without `forall T` — the error names the binder and # writes out the line you meant. # # * `impl Show for Box(Int32)` — iyi has no specialised impls. Overlapping # impls need a rule for which one wins, and that rule has to stay sound when # the two live in modules compiled separately; Rust has wanted this for a # decade and it is still unstable, and Java cannot express it at all. # Refusing it is what keeps `Box(T)`'s method set knowable without knowing T. # # * `impl Show for T forall T : Show` — a blanket impl, refused for the reason # open classes are: it lets a distant module add methods to every type. # # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Not yet implemented # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * `forall T : Show` parses but is rejected. A bound makes the impl # conditional, and a conditional impl has to be checked where the type is # instantiated rather than where the impl is written. # # * Under R-4 an impl on a generic type should be compiled once per GC shape # rather than once per instantiation. Today this monomorphises, exactly the # way Crystal does. # # * Two impls of the same *parameterised* trait for one type collide when their # methods take the same arguments: `impl Into(String) for U` and # `impl Into(Int32) for U` both define `into`, and the second silently wins. # Parameters exist for exactly this case, so it needs an answer — Rust's is # to pick the impl from the type the call site expects.
files.samples/iyi/hello.iyi: # The first iyi program. # # ./bin/crystal run samples/iyi/hello.iyi # # Everything below compiles and runs today. What is still missing is listed at # the bottom — this file is meant to stay honest about how far the # implementation actually reaches. # R-1: the compilation-unit header. A module is the unit of compilation and of # recompilation; `import` edges between modules form a DAG. Reading a module's # `.iyimod` is what will one day replace re-analysing its source. module samples/hello # R-3: a trait is a named set of requirements. `abstract def` marks a method an # implementer must provide. Traits replace Crystal's open classes: a type's # method set is knowable without reading the whole program. pub trait Greet abstract def greet : String end pub trait Loud abstract def shout : String end # R-2: `pub` marks a declaration as exported, and exported declarations carry # full signatures. That signature is the module's contract, and the only thing # a consumer ever needs to read. pub struct User getter name : String def initialize(@name : String) end end pub struct Robot getter id : Int32 def initialize(@id : Int32) end end # `impl Trait for Type` — the replacement for reopening a class. R-3's orphan # rule requires it to live in the module defining either the trait or the # type, and that is enforced: both are defined right here. `modules.iyi` shows # the cross-module case, where the choice actually costs something. impl Greet for User def greet : String "Hello, #{name}!" end end # A type may implement several traits... impl Loud for User def shout : String greet.upcase end end # ...and a trait may be implemented by several types. impl Greet for Robot def greet : String "BEEP #{id}" end end # `impl` is the only way to give a type a trait. SPEC.md II.8 — each of these # is refused, and each for its own reason: # # struct User # include Greet # a type acquires a trait by having an impl, whose # end # location R-3 can check; `include` has no such rule # # using samples/hello/greet # a trait exports no names to bring into # # scope — a trait method is resolved from the # # receiver, never from a `using` # # impl Greet for Loud # a blanket impl in disguise # # And leaving a requirement unmet is an error where the impl is written, not # where the type is later used: # # impl Loud for Robot # end # # => impl Loud for Robot is missing a method required by the trait: shout # Not exported. No signature required, because nothing outside this module can # depend on it — inference inside a module costs only what the module costs. def describe(item) item.greet end # A trait bound on a method's own type parameter — SPEC.md II.7 rule 3. The # method exists for every `T`; the bound is checked where `T` binds, so a call # with a type that does not implement `Greet` is rejected at that call: # # announce(42) # # => Int32 does not implement Samples::Hello::Greet, required by `T` # # in `announce` # # This is the shape Kemal's router needs: `&block : Context -> B forall # B : IntoBody` replaces a per-request runtime type check with one at compile # time. Note this is *not* the impl-level bound below — nothing here is # conditional. pub def announce(item : T) : String forall T : Greet "-> #{item.greet}" end # Ruby ergonomics, unchanged and free to compile: blocks, string # interpolation, everything-is-an-expression, local inference. puts User.new("iyi").greet puts User.new("iyi").shout puts Robot.new(42).greet # A trait as a type: both implementers dispatch through it. crowd = [User.new("crystal"), Robot.new(7)] of Greet crowd.each { |member| puts describe(member) } puts announce(Robot.new(9)) # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Not yet implemented # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * Trait bounds on a generic *impl*'s parameters (`impl Show for Box(T) # forall T : Show`) parse but are rejected — unlike the bound on `announce` # above, which works. A bound on an impl makes the impl conditional: # `Box(Int32)` would implement `Show` only if `Int32` did, which has to be # checked where the type is instantiated rather than where the impl is # written. A different mechanism, and the harder of the two. # # * Dictionary-passing generics is unimplemented: `announce` above is # monomorphised the way Crystal monomorphises it. # # * `.iyimod` reaches the front end and stops there. `modules.iyi` and # `immutable.iyi` compile with the imported module's source deleted, but a # build that reads artifacts cannot yet produce a program, because the # artifact carries declarations and no object code (SPEC.md IV.1f). # # * The prelude under this file is iyi's own, 833 lines of it, and that is why # building it costs 0.32 s rather than 2.10 s. It is not a standard library # and does not pretend to be one: no `Float64#to_s`, no `Range`, no `Set`, # no formatting, and `raise` is a panic that prints and exits. What is in it # is what a sample called for (SPEC.md, "0.1.0", item 3). # # See `modules.iyi` for `import` and `using` across files, `generics.iyi` for # implementing a trait for a generic type and for associated types, bounds and # requirements, and `collections.iyi` for `Enumerable` ported onto all of it.
files.samples/iyi/immutable.iyi: # The shareable immutable sequence, exercised — SPEC.md III.4.7. # # ./bin/crystal run samples/iyi/immutable.iyi # # `std/list.iyi` holds the type. This file is the evidence for the two claims # made about it, because a type that merely compiles has proved neither: # # * It is genuinely immutable — nothing a caller keeps a hold of can change # a list after it exists, which is what makes it shareable under III.4.4. # * It costs one `each` and gets the rest, which is II.6's claim tested on a # second type after `Enumerable` itself, and the first time on a *generic* # one. module samples/immutable import std/list using std/list::{List} # Two ways of naming the same type, both across a module boundary. The second # lets the argument be inferred, and it is written that way on purpose: the # artifact carries no machine code for a generic, so `List(String)` is a type # this file makes, and inference puts `new` on `List(T)` instead of on the # instance. That difference once linked undefined and nothing here caught it, # because every line in this file wrote the argument out. nums = List(Int32).new([3, 1, 4, 1, 5]) words = List.new(["pear", "fig", "plum", "kiwi"]) # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Its own surface: small on purpose # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- puts "size #{nums.size}" puts "empty? #{nums.empty?} #{List(Int32).new([] of Int32).empty?}" puts "at #{nums.at(0)} #{nums.at(4)}" # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Immutability, demonstrated rather than asserted # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # `appended` returns a new list and leaves this one alone. By III.1.7 the plain # verb names the mutating form, so the participle is the only name this type # can have — `push` and `sort` describe something it cannot do. The naming # convention was settled before any library code existed precisely so that it # would fall out here rather than be applied here. longer = nums.appended(9) puts "appended #{longer.size} from #{nums.size}, original #{nums.to_a.join(",")}" puts "concatenated #{nums.concatenated(List(Int32).new([7])).to_a.join(",")} / #{nums.size}" # The constructor copies, and this is the line that shows why it must. `source` # is still held by this file; if the list had kept it rather than copying, a # task holding `taken` would see it change underneath. That copy is the price # of having no borrow checker to say "I own this now" — one copy, at the # boundary, once. source = [1, 2] taken = List(Int32).new(source) source << 3 puts "copied list #{taken.size}, source #{source.size}" # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Everything below here is the trait's, from one `each` # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- puts "to_a #{nums.to_a.join(",")}" puts "all?/any? #{nums.all? { |x| x > 0 }} #{nums.any? { |x| x > 4 }}" puts "none?/one? #{nums.none? { |x| x > 9 }} #{nums.one? { |x| x == 4 }}" puts "count #{nums.count { |x| x == 1 }}" puts "find?/find #{nums.find? { |x| x > 3 }} #{nums.find { |x| x > 3 }}" puts "index?/index #{nums.index? { |x| x == 4 }} #{nums.index { |x| x == 4 }}" puts "first?/first #{nums.first?} #{nums.first}" puts "map #{nums.map { |x| x * 2 }.join(",")}" puts "flat_map #{nums.flat_map { |x| [x, x] }.join(",")}" puts "map_with_index #{nums.map_with_index { |x, i| x * i }.join(",")}" puts "select/reject #{nums.select { |x| x > 2 }.join(",")} #{nums.reject { |x| x > 2 }.join(",")}" puts "partition #{nums.partition { |x| x > 2 }.map(&.join("+")).join(" | ")}" puts "take/skip #{nums.take(2).join(",")} #{nums.skip(3).join(",")}" puts "take_while #{nums.take_while { |x| x < 4 }.join(",")}" puts "skip_while #{nums.skip_while { |x| x < 4 }.join(",")}" puts "reduce #{nums.reduce(0) { |a, x| a + x }}" puts "each_with_object #{nums.each_with_object([] of Int32) { |o, e| o << e * 10 }.join(",")}" puts "join #{nums.join("-")}" puts "includes? #{nums.includes?(4)} #{nums.includes?(9)}" puts "max/min #{nums.max} #{nums.min}" puts "sum/product #{nums.sum} #{nums.product}" puts "tally #{nums.tally[1]}" puts "sorted #{nums.sorted.join(",")}" puts "max_by #{words.max_by { |s| s.size }}" puts "group_by #{words.group_by { |s| s.size }[4].join(",")}" # The trait reaches a generic type, which is the part that was not built until # this file needed it. `type Elem = T` binds the associated type to the impl's # own parameter, so `List(Int32)` enumerates `Int32` and `List(String)` # enumerates `String` from the same impl — II.6 × II.7, which had never met. puts "two elem types #{nums.map { |x| x + 1 }.join(",")} / #{words.map { |s| s.size }.join(",")}" # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # All of the above, with `samples/iyi/std` deleted # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # ./bin/crystal build --no-codegen --emit-iyimod /tmp/mods samples/iyi/immutable.iyi # mv samples/iyi/std /tmp/std-elsewhere # ./bin/crystal build --use-iyimod /tmp/mods samples/iyi/immutable.iyi # compiles # mv /tmp/std-elsewhere samples/iyi/std # # This file is the hard case for R-1's contract, not `modules.iyi`: what has to # survive the round trip is a generic struct, a 575-line trait with an # associated type, and a generic impl that answers it. `mod dump --declarations # /tmp/mods/std/list.iyimod` is what the second build reads — the six headers # with no bodies, and `impl … for Std::List::List(T) forall T` with its # `type Elem = T`. Every call above is checked against those and against # nothing else (SPEC.md IV.1f). # # Not codegen: `--use-iyimod` implies `--no-codegen`, so this compiles the file # without producing a program. `./bin/crystal run` above is still an ordinary # build that reads the sources.
files.samples/iyi/init_order.iyi: # Module initialisation order: SPEC.md III.5. # # ./bin/crystal run samples/iyi/init_order.iyi # # Prints its five lines in the order they are numbered, and the numbering is # the whole point — none of it comes from where the `import` directives are # written. A module's top-level expressions are its initialiser (rule 3), and # a module initialises after every module it imports (rule 1). module samples/init_order # Written above the imports on purpose, and it still runs after both modules # below have initialised. The compiler holds a module's initialiser apart from # the site that imported it and puts them in the order the import DAG forces: # `boot/config` before `boot/registry` because the second imports the first, # and this file last because it imports both. puts "4. samples/init_order, above its own `import` lines" import boot/registry import boot/config puts "5. #{Boot::Registry.greeting}" # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # What this sample does not promise # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * The order of two modules that do not import each other. Rule 2 says that # order is *unobservable*, not merely unspecified — a module can only name # what it imports (R-1), reach what that module exports (R-2), and reopen # nothing (R-3), so an initialiser has nothing of an unrelated module to # look at. Nothing here prints from two independent modules, because that # would be documenting an order the spec refuses to have — and debug builds # shuffle it, so the documentation would be wrong most of the time. Build # with `--release` to get the load order back, or `IYI_INIT_SEED=1` to get # the same shuffled one twice. # # * Anything about the second `import` above. `boot/config` was already loaded # by `boot/registry`, so naming it here adds an edge and nothing else: a # module imported by several others is compiled once and initialised once. # # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # What this sample would report as an error # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * A top-level expression that propagates an error with `!`. Initialisation # may not fail (rule 4): if it can fail it is not initialisation, it is work, # and work belongs in a function the program calls when it is ready to handle # the failure. The error names III.5. # # * An import cycle. `import` forms a DAG (R-1), and a cycle has no order that # satisfies rule 1 — each module would have to initialise after the other. # The error names the cycle. Adding `import boot/registry` to `boot/config` # reports `boot/registry -> boot/config -> boot/registry`, the chain as it # was walked, not as it was written. # # * An `import` inside a `def` — `can't import inside def`, reported by the # parser. Inside any other expression the semantic pass reports `can't import # dynamically` instead. Rule 1 needs the import graph to be a DAG the # compiler can see before it runs anything. # # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Not yet implemented # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * A module's initialiser as something an artifact could store. The compiler # holds the modules' *nodes* apart from their import sites, which is what # rules 1 and 2 needed, but `.iyimod` needs the step after: a callable # initialiser in the module's own object code (SPEC.md Part IV).
files.samples/iyi/kemal/dsl.iyi: # Kemal's DSL, ported from `kemal/src/kemal/dsl.cr`. # # The original's first line is the whole problem: "Kemal DSL is defined here # and it's baked into global scope." `require "kemal"` injects `get`, `post` # and `before_all` into the importing program's namespace — the same action at # a distance as an open class, and also Kemal's entire identity. Making users # write `kemal.get "/" do ... end` would be safe and would kill the framework. # # `using` moves the decision to the consumer: the library exports names, and # the program says which ones it wants unqualified. See `webapp.iyi`. module kemal/dsl import kemal/router using kemal/router::{Router, Context, IntoBody} HTTP_METHODS = %w(get post put patch delete options head) # One application value, in place of `Kemal::RouteHandler::INSTANCE` and the # three singletons beside it. `router.cr:270` works around those being global # and mutable — "may have been cleared between tests" — and nothing about # separate compilation forced that; a clean sheet is just the moment to fix it. APP = Router.new {% for method in HTTP_METHODS %} pub def {{ method.id }}(path : String, &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody APP.{{ method.id }}(path, &block) end {% end %} pub def before_all(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody APP.before(path, &block) end pub def after_all(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody APP.after(path, &block) end pub def mount(path : String, router : Router) : Nil APP.mount(path, router) end pub def app : Router APP end
files.samples/iyi/kemal/router.iyi: # Kemal's modular router, ported to iyi from `kemal/src/kemal/router.cr` (337 # lines). This is the acceptance test the design named: the hardest DSL in the # Crystal ecosystem for "no open classes, no global macros". # # What is deliberately not ported, and why: # # * `HTTP::Server::Context`, WebSocket and SSE — they need the stdlib, and # they add no construct the routes do not already exercise. `Context` here # is a stub. # * `Kemal::RouteHandler::INSTANCE` and the other global mutable singletons. # `router.cr:270` carries a workaround for them — "may have been cleared # between tests" — and a clean sheet is the moment to stop. Registration # returns a value instead. module kemal/router pub struct Context getter method : String getter path : String def initialize(@method : String, @path : String) end end # The finding the port produced. Kemal types a route block as # `HTTP::Server::Context -> _` and coerces the result on every request: # # result = block.call(ctx) # result.is_a?(String) ? result : "" # router.cr:301 # # Mandatory export signatures forbid `_`, so the block's return type has to be # named — and once it is named, the coercion becomes a bound. The check moves # from every request to compile time, and a user can now make their own type # returnable by implementing the trait, which Kemal cannot offer. pub trait IntoBody abstract def into_body : String end impl IntoBody for String def into_body : String self end end impl IntoBody for Nil def into_body : String "" end end impl IntoBody for Int32 def into_body : String to_s end end HTTP_METHODS = %w(get post put patch delete options head) FILTER_METHODS = %w(get post put patch delete options) pub class Router alias Handler = Context -> String private record RouteDefinition, method : String, path : String, handler : Handler private record FilterDefinition, kind : Symbol, method : String, path : String, handler : Handler private record SubRouter, path : String, router : Router getter prefix : String @routes : Array(RouteDefinition) @filters : Array(FilterDefinition) @sub_routers : Array(SubRouter) def initialize(@prefix : String = "") @routes = [] of RouteDefinition @filters = [] of FilterDefinition @sub_routers = [] of SubRouter end # The macro loop ports unchanged — it reads a module-local constant and # emits declarations into its own module, which is legal under R-5. The one # addition is `forall B : IntoBody` on each generated signature. {% for method in HTTP_METHODS %} pub def {{ method.id }}(path : String, &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody add_route({{ method.upcase }}, path, &block) end {% end %} pub def before(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody add_filter(:before, "ALL", path, &block) end pub def after(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody add_filter(:after, "ALL", path, &block) end {% for method in FILTER_METHODS %} pub def before_{{ method.id }}(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody add_filter(:before, {{ method.upcase }}, path, &block) end pub def after_{{ method.id }}(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody add_filter(:after, {{ method.upcase }}, path, &block) end {% end %} # The sub-router arrives as a block parameter, and Kemal's original hands it # to the block as `self` instead — `with sub_router yield`. That is the one # thing about this port that reads worse than what it ports, so the reason is # here rather than in a commit message. # # R-2 asks an exported `def` to say what its block is (SPEC.md IV.2): the # body stays in this module, so a consumer reading only the signature has no # `yield` left to infer from. `& : Router -> Nil` says it. `with sub_router # yield` cannot be said at all — what makes it a DSL is that the block's # `self` changes, and `& : … -> …` has nowhere to write that down. # # So this is the rule costing something visible, and it is being paid rather # than avoided: a `namespace` that keeps `with` would have to stay unexported, # which is a worse trade for a DSL than one extra `|r|`. Giving `with … yield` # a notation is open (SPEC.md IV.2); until it has one, this is what an # exported block-taking method looks like. pub def namespace(path : String, & : Router -> Nil) : Nil sub_router = Router.new yield sub_router @sub_routers << SubRouter.new(path: path, router: sub_router) end pub def mount(path : String, router : Router) : Nil @sub_routers << SubRouter.new(path: path, router: router) end # Kemal's `register_routes` pushed into global singletons. This returns the # flattened table instead, which is the same walk without the globals. pub def routes(base_prefix : String = "") : Array(Tuple(String, String)) full_prefix = join_paths(base_prefix, @prefix) collected = [] of Tuple(String, String) @routes.each do |route| collected << {route.method, join_paths(full_prefix, route.path)} end @sub_routers.each do |sub| collected.concat(sub.router.routes(join_paths(full_prefix, sub.path))) end collected end # Ported from `register_filters`, which is the densest code in the file: # `case` on a symbol, `select` destructuring a tuple, `in?` over a splat, # and `starts_with?`. pub def filters_for(method : String, path : String) : Array(Symbol) applicable = [] of Symbol @filters.each do |filter| next unless filter.method.in?("ALL", method) matches = if filter.path == "*" true else scoped = join_paths(@prefix, filter.path) path == scoped || path.starts_with?("#{scoped}/") end next unless matches case filter.kind when :before then applicable << :before when :after then applicable << :after end end applicable end pub def dispatch(ctx : Context) : String before = 0 after = 0 filters_for(ctx.method, ctx.path).each do |kind| case kind when :before then before += 1 when :after then after += 1 end end body = "" @routes.each do |route| if route.method == ctx.method && join_paths(@prefix, route.path) == ctx.path body = route.handler.call(ctx) end end @sub_routers.each do |sub| body = sub.router.dispatch(ctx) if body.empty? end "#{before}|#{body}|#{after}" end private def add_route(method : String, path : String, &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody handler = ->(ctx : Context) { block.call(ctx).into_body } @routes << RouteDefinition.new(method: method, path: path, handler: handler) end private def add_filter(kind : Symbol, method : String, path : String, &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody handler = ->(ctx : Context) { block.call(ctx).into_body } @filters << FilterDefinition.new(kind: kind, method: method, path: path, handler: handler) end private def join_paths(a : String, b : String) : String a = a.chomp('/') b = b.lchop('/') if b.starts_with?('/') return "/#{b}" if a.empty? return a if b.empty? "#{a}/#{b}" end end
