It brings the module into scope # under its qualified name and nothing more — after this line, and with no # `using`, the module's names are reachable only as `App::Greeter::Greet` and # `App::Greeter.polite`. import app/greeter import app/formal # II.3: `using` is what makes those names available unqualified. It is written # by the consumer, not performed by the library: importing a module never # changes what the importer's unqualified names mean, so a library cannot # capture a name in your file by adding one to itself. using app/greeter # The selective form narrows a `using` to the names listed. Here it is not # decoration — `app/greeter` and `app/formal` both export `title`, and taking # both whole would make every unqualified `title` in this module ambiguous. using app/formal::{address} pub struct User getter name : String def initialize(@name : String) end end # `Greet` resolves through the `using` above, so `impl` needs no qualification. # # R-3's orphan rule allows this impl here because `User` is declared here: # this is the type's module. It would equally be allowed in `app/greeter`, # the trait's module. Nowhere else — a third module that imports both is # refused, which is what makes two modules unable to define the same impl. impl Greet for User def greet : String # `polite` comes from `app/greeter`, `address` from `app/formal`, and # `shout` is this module's own function, declared below. All three are # written the same way, because to this file they are all just names. shout(polite(name)) + " " + address(name) end end # A module's own functions are in scope for the types declared in it, without # `self.` and without qualification: an iyi module is a compilation unit, and # these are its functions. Not exported, so nothing outside can call it. def shout(text : String) : String text.upcase end puts User.new("iyi").greet # `title` was reachable unqualified from neither `using`: `app/greeter`'s was # left ambiguous by nothing (only one `using` was whole), and `app/formal`'s # was excluded by the selective form. Qualification always works. puts App::Greeter.title puts App::Formal.title # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # What this sample would report as an error # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * Widening the second directive to `using app/formal` and then writing an # unqualified `title` is an error, and it is reported at the `title`, not at # the `using`. Widening it alone is not an error at all: two modules # exporting the same name is not by itself a mistake, so nothing is wrong # until a name is written that could mean either (SPEC.md II.3). # # * Adding `def title` here makes even that legal again. A local definition # beats a used one, silently, which is what keeps a library from breaking # its consumers by adding an export. # # * Moving the `impl` above into a module that is neither `app/greeter` nor # this one is refused by R-3, naming both modules where it would be allowed. # # * `using app/greeter::{greeting}` — `greeting` is declared there without # `pub`, so it is not part of the module's surface. The error names it at the # `using`, where the author can see which of the names they asked for they # cannot have. Widening to a bare `using app/greeter` does not reach it # either; it simply is not there to be found (R-2b). # # * `App::Greeter.greeting` — qualifying it does not get around `pub` either. # It has to be unreachable, not merely absent from `using`: `.iyimod` carries # a module's exports and nothing else, so if another module could call an # unmarked name, that metadata would not be enough to compile against # (SPEC.md IV.2). # # * `import app/v_1`, or any path segment that is not `[a-z][a-z0-9]*` with # single `_` between groups. A module declared `app/greeter` is reached as # `App::Greeter`, and the two notations are kept in step by making the # mapping reversible: the name splits back into a path at every upper-case # letter. `camelcase` drops an underscore before a digit, so `v_1` and `v1` # would both be `V1` — two paths naming one module (SPEC.md IV.6 #6). # # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Compiling this file without `app/greeter.iyi` # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # R-1 says a module that imports another reads its `.iyimod` and never opens # its source. That is not a claim about a future release: # # ./bin/crystal build --no-codegen --emit-iyimod /tmp/mods samples/iyi/modules.iyi # ./bin/crystal mod dump --declarations /tmp/mods/app/greeter.iyimod # mv samples/iyi/app /tmp/app-elsewhere # ./bin/crystal build --use-iyimod /tmp/mods samples/iyi/modules.iyi # compiles # mv /tmp/app-elsewhere samples/iyi/app # # The second command prints what the third one compiles against: `app/greeter` # with `pub def polite(name : String) : String`, `pub trait Greet` with its # requirement, and no bodies at all. `greeting` is not in it — it carries no # `pub`, and R-2b's "unreachable rather than absent from `using`" is the same # statement as "not in the artifact". # # * Not yet: object code. `--use-iyimod` implies `--no-codegen`, because the # artifact carries what another module may call and not how it is done, so # there is nothing in it to generate a program from (SPEC.md IV.1f).
files.samples/iyi/std/derives.iyi: # Derives, as a library module (SPEC.md R-5, II.4). # # A derive is an exported macro that takes one argument: the declaration it is # attached to. It reads that declaration's name and its fields, each field with # the type it was written as. It never sees a type it was not given, and it # never runs in the consumer. module std/derives pub trait Show abstract def show : String end # A type this module exports, implementing a trait this module exports. A derive # in another module gets to ask about both, and both arrive from this module's # `.iyimod` when its source is gone. pub struct Name @text : String def initialize(@text : String) end end impl Show for Name def show : String "<" + @text + ">" end end # Renders a value as its type name and its fields. One macro, any declaration: # the fields come from whichever type the derive is written in. pub macro described(declaration) def described : String result = {{declaration[:name]}} + "(" {% for field in declaration[:fields] %} result = result + {{field[:name]}} + "=" + {{field[:name].id}}.to_s + " " {% end %} result + ")" end end # The question II.4 is about: whether a field's type implements a trait. Only # the fields that answer yes are rendered, and each one is rendered by calling # the trait's method. A field whose type this macro cannot see answers `nil`. pub macro shown(declaration) def shown : String result = "" {% for field in declaration[:fields] %} {% if field[:type] && field[:type] <= Show %} result = result + {{field[:name]}} + "=" + {{field[:name].id}}.show + " " {% end %} {% end %} result end end
files.samples/iyi/std/enumerable.iyi: # `Enumerable`, ported — SPEC.md II.6. # # The load-bearing abstraction of Crystal's standard library: 71 method names # in 117 defs, written against a single `abstract def each`, included by 17 # types. If traits # cannot express this shape, the library cannot be written in Crystal's idiom # and the ergonomics half of the pitch fails. So this file is the evidence for # the claim, not an illustration of it. # # ./bin/crystal run samples/iyi/collections.iyi # # 57 of those 71 names are here, in 58 defs. Every one of them is called by # `collections.iyi`, because a default method that is never called is never # typed — compiling this file proves nothing on its own. # # It needs all three of what II.6 said it would need, and nothing else: # # * `type Elem` — an associated type. The element type is an output of the # impl, not something the caller picks. Were it a parameter, one type could # implement `Enumerable(String)` and `Enumerable(Int32)` and `arr.map` # would be ambiguous about which impl it meant. # * `forall U` on methods — `map`, `flat_map`, `group_by`, `min_by`, # `reduce`, `accumulate` and eight more. `U` belongs to the method, not to # the trait. # * `where Elem : Cmp` — about a quarter of `Enumerable` is valid only for # some element types. `max`, `min`, `sum`, `product`, `tally`, `sorted`, # `includes?` and `minmax` say so instead of duck-typing. `sum` and # `product` also need `Num` to require `self.zero` and `self.one`: an # identity belongs to the type, since an empty collection has no element # to ask. # # What the port corrected in the spec's own sketch: # # * II.6 writes `abstract def each(&block : Elem -> Nil)`. That form # *captures* the block into a `Proc`, and a captured block cannot `return` # from the enclosing method — which kills early exit in `find`, `any?`, # `all?`, `none?`, `first`, `take`, `take_while`, `empty?`, `index` and # `find_value`. The block has to be typed without being captured, as # `& : Elem -> Nil`, and yielded. That is the form the Crystal stdlib uses # for the same reason. # * Crystal spells two of these `find!` and `index!`. With `!` out of # identifiers (III.1.7) the port takes the convention `Enumerable` already # uses everywhere else — `max?`/`max`, `first?`/`first` — and applies it # here too: `?` is the nilable one, the plain name raises. Dropping `!` # made the library *more* consistent, not less. module std/enumerable import std/traits using std/traits::{Cmp, Num, Hashable} pub trait Enumerable type Elem abstract def each(& : Elem -> Nil) : Nil # ---- building ------------------------------------------------------------ def to_a : Array(Elem) result = [] of Elem each { |e| result << e } result end def size : Int32 n = 0 each { |e| n = n + 1 } n end def empty? : Bool each { |e| return false } true end # ---- predicates ---------------------------------------------------------- def all?(& : Elem -> Bool) : Bool each { |e| return false unless yield e } true end def any?(& : Elem -> Bool) : Bool each { |e| return true if yield e } false end def none?(& : Elem -> Bool) : Bool each { |e| return false if yield e } true end def one?(& : Elem -> Bool) : Bool found = false each do |e| if yield e return false if found found = true end end found end def count(& : Elem -> Bool) : Int32 n = 0 each { |e| n = n + 1 if yield e } n end # ---- searching ----------------------------------------------------------- # # Crystal spells these `find` (nilable) and `find!` (raises). With `!` out of # identifiers, the port takes the convention `Enumerable` already uses # everywhere else — `max?`/`max`, `first?`/`first` — and applies it here too: # `?` is the nilable one, the plain name is the one that raises. def find?(& : Elem -> Bool) : Elem? each { |e| return e if yield e } nil end def find(& : Elem -> Bool) : Elem each { |e| return e if yield e } raise "no element matched" end def index?(& : Elem -> Bool) : Int32? i = 0 each do |e| return i if yield e i = i + 1 end nil end def index(& : Elem -> Bool) : Int32 i = 0 each do |e| return i if yield e i = i + 1 end raise "no element matched" end def first? : Elem? each { |e| return e } nil end def first : Elem each { |e| return e } raise "empty" end # ---- transforming -------------------------------------------------------- # # `U` belongs to the method, not to the trait: `map` is one method that works # for every result type, not one trait per result type (SPEC.md II.6). def map(& : Elem -> U) : Array(U) forall U result = [] of U each { |e| result << yield e } result end def flat_map(& : Elem -> Array(U)) : Array(U) forall U result = [] of U each { |e| (yield e).each { |inner| result << inner } } result end def map_with_index(& : Elem, Int32 -> U) : Array(U) forall U result = [] of U i = 0 each do |e| result << yield e, i i = i + 1 end result end def select(& : Elem -> Bool) : Array(Elem) result = [] of Elem each { |e| result << e if yield e } result end def reject(& : Elem -> Bool) : Array(Elem) result = [] of Elem each { |e| result << e unless yield e } result end def partition(& : Elem -> Bool) : Array(Array(Elem)) yes = [] of Elem no = [] of Elem each do |e| if yield e yes << e else no << e end end [yes, no] end def take(n : Int32) : Array(Elem) result = [] of Elem each do |e| return result if result.size >= n result << e end result end def skip(n : Int32) : Array(Elem) result = [] of Elem i = 0 each do |e| result << e if i >= n i = i + 1 end result end def take_while(& : Elem -> Bool) : Array(Elem) result = [] of Elem each do |e| return result unless yield e result << e end result end def skip_while(& : Elem -> Bool) : Array(Elem) result = [] of Elem skipping = true each do |e| skipping = false if skipping && !yield e result << e unless skipping end result end # ---- folding ------------------------------------------------------------- def reduce(initial : U, & : U, Elem -> U) : U forall U acc = initial each { |e| acc = yield acc, e } acc end def each_with_index(& : Elem, Int32 -> Nil) : Nil i = 0 each do |e| yield e, i i = i + 1 end end def each_with_object(obj : U, & : U, Elem -> Nil) : U forall U each { |e| yield obj, e } obj end def join(separator : String) : String result = "" first = true each do |e| result = result + separator unless first result = result + e.to_s first = false end result end # ---- needing something of the element type ------------------------------- # # About a quarter of `Enumerable` is valid only for some element types. This # is where `where` earns its place: the trait says so, instead of duck-typing # and failing at instantiation with a message naming neither the bound nor # the element type. def includes?(value : Elem) : Bool where Elem : Cmp each { |e| return true if e.cmp(value) == 0 } false end def max? : Elem? where Elem : Cmp best = nil each do |e| current = best best = e if current.nil? || e.gt(current) end best end def max : Elem where Elem : Cmp found = max? return found unless found.nil? raise "empty" end def min? : Elem? where Elem : Cmp best = nil each do |e| current = best best = e if current.nil? || e.lt(current) end best end def min : Elem where Elem : Cmp found = min? return found unless found.nil? raise "empty" end def sum : Elem where Elem : Num acc = Elem.zero each { |e| acc = acc.add(e) } acc end def product : Elem where Elem : Num acc = Elem.one each { |e| acc = acc.mul(e) } acc end def tally : Hash(Elem, Int32) where Elem : Hashable counts = {} of Elem => Int32 each { |e| counts[e] = (counts[e]? || 0) + 1 } counts end def sorted : Array(Elem) where Elem : Cmp to_a.sorted { |a, b| a.cmp(b) } end # ---- needing something of the block's result type ------------------------- def max_by(& : Elem -> U) : Elem forall U : Cmp best = nil best_key = nil each do |e| key = yield e current = best_key if current.nil? || key.gt(current) best = e best_key = key end end found = best return found unless found.nil? raise "empty" end def group_by(& : Elem -> U) : Hash(U, Array(Elem)) forall U : Hashable groups = {} of U => Array(Elem) each do |e| key = yield e bucket = groups[key]? if bucket.nil? groups[key] = [e] else bucket << e end end groups end def index_by(& : Elem -> U) : Hash(U, Elem) forall U : Hashable result = {} of U => Elem each { |e| result[yield e] = e } result end def each_slice(n : Int32) : Array(Array(Elem)) slices = [] of Array(Elem) current = [] of Elem each do |e| current << e if current.size == n slices << current current = [] of Elem end end slices << current unless current.empty? slices end def each_cons(n : Int32) : Array(Array(Elem)) result = [] of Array(Elem) window = [] of Elem each do |e| window << e window.shift if window.size > n result << window.dup if window.size == n end result end def chunk_while(& : Elem, Elem -> Bool) : Array(Array(Elem)) chunks = [] of Array(Elem) current = [] of Elem previous = nil each do |e| last = previous if last.nil? || (yield last, e) current << e else chunks << current current = [e] end previous = e end chunks << current unless current.empty? chunks end def cycle(n : Int32, & : Elem -> Nil) : Nil i = 0 while i < n each { |e| yield e } i = i + 1 end end def first(n : Int32) : Array(Elem) take(n) end def compact_map(& : Elem -> U?) : Array(U) forall U result = [] of U each do |e| value = yield e result << value unless value.nil? end result end def find_value(& : Elem -> U?) : U? forall U each do |e| value = yield e return value unless value.nil? end nil end def accumulate(initial : U, & : U, Elem -> U) : Array(U) forall U acc = initial result = [acc] each do |e| acc = yield acc, e result << acc end result end def reduce?(& : Elem, Elem -> Elem) : Elem? acc = nil each do |e| current = acc acc = current.nil? ? e : (yield current, e) end acc end def in_groups_of(n : Int32, filler : Elem) : Array(Array(Elem)) groups = each_slice(n) last = groups.last? if last while last.size < n last << filler end end groups end def zip(other : O) : Array(Tuple(Elem, O::Elem)) forall O : Enumerable # SPEC.md II.6 finding 6: Crystal's # `zip(*others : Indexable | Iterable | Iterator)` is duck typing left over # from having no traits. One bound replaces the union, and `O::Elem` names # what the other collection yields without the caller stating it. theirs = other.to_a result = [] of Tuple(Elem, O::Elem) i = 0 each do |e| result << {e, theirs[i]} if i < theirs.size i = i + 1 end result end def min_by(& : Elem -> U) : Elem forall U : Cmp best = nil best_key = nil each do |e| key = yield e current = best_key if current.nil? || key.lt(current) best = e best_key = key end end found = best return found unless found.nil? raise "empty" end def max_of(& : Elem -> U) : U forall U : Cmp best = nil each do |e| key = yield e current = best best = key if current.nil? || key.gt(current) end found = best return found unless found.nil? raise "empty" end def min_of(& : Elem -> U) : U forall U : Cmp best = nil each do |e| key = yield e current = best best = key if current.nil? || key.lt(current) end found = best return found unless found.nil? raise "empty" end def minmax : Tuple(Elem, Elem) where Elem : Cmp low = min high = max {low, high} end def tally_by(& : Elem -> U) : Hash(U, Int32) forall U : Hashable counts = {} of U => Int32 each do |e| key = yield e counts[key] = (counts[key]? || 0) + 1 end counts end def sum_by(& : Elem -> U) : U forall U : Num acc = U.zero each { |e| acc = acc.add(yield e) } acc end end # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Not ported, and why # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * `to_h`, `chunks`, `in_slices_of` — they destructure the element as a pair # or a tuple, which needs the element type to be constrained to a shape # rather than to a trait. # # * `sample`, `each_step`, `step` — `Random` and numeric stepping, neither of # which is about `Enumerable`. # # * `max_by?`, `min_by?`, `minmax_by`, `minmax_of`, `max_of?` and the rest of # the nilable-variant family. They are mechanical repeats of the ones here # and would prove nothing further. # # * Crystal's specialisations, where `Indexable` overrides `size` or `first` # with an O(1) version. That is II.6's `@[Monomorphize]` question and the # dictionary-passing design, neither of which is implemented.
files.samples/iyi/std/list.iyi: # `List`, the shareable immutable sequence — SPEC.md III.4.7. # # ./bin/crystal run samples/iyi/immutable.iyi # # This exists because a count said it had to. III.4.7 measured what `Share` # would cost and found clean-sheet iyi code 77% shareable as written — and that # **every** failure in it was a type holding an `Array`. With no shareable # collection the only way past the marker is `Mutex(Array(T))` everywhere, and # an escape hatch used routinely is the definition of a failed rule. So the # standard library owes the language this type; it is not a convenience. # # It is also the second test of II.6's claim, after `Enumerable` itself: one # `each`, and the trait supplies the rest. module std/list import std/enumerable using std/enumerable::{Enumerable} # The store is built at construction and never handed out, so no method of this # type can be observed to change it. That is what makes the value shareable # under III.4.4 — every field immutable after construction — and it is why the # constructor **copies**. # # The copy is not defensive habit, it is the missing borrow checker. `List` # cannot express "I own this array now", so a caller that kept a reference to # what it passed in could mutate the list from underneath a task holding it. # Rust says this with ownership and pays nothing; here it costs one copy at the # boundary, once, and it is the honest price of not having that machinery. pub struct List(T) @items : Array(T) def initialize(items : Array(T)) @items = items.dup end def size : Int32 @items.size end def empty? : Bool @items.empty? end def at(index : Int32) : T @items[index] end # Every operation that would change a sequence returns a new one instead, so # by III.1.7's convention they are all participles. The plain verbs — `push`, # `sort`, `reverse` — name the mutating form, and this type has none. That the # naming rule falls out rather than being applied is the point of having # settled it before any library code existed. def appended(item : T) : List(T) copy = @items.dup copy << item List(T).new(copy) end def concatenated(other : List(T)) : List(T) copy = @items.dup other.each { |x| copy << x } List(T).new(copy) end end # The whole surface below `each` comes from the trait. `Elem` is bound to the # impl's own parameter, which is the associated type doing exactly what II.6 # said it was for: the element type is an output of the impl, not something a # caller picks. impl Enumerable for List(T) forall T type Elem = T def each(& : T -> Nil) : Nil @items.each { |x| yield x } end end
files.samples/iyi/std/traits.iyi: module std/traits pub trait Cmp abstract def cmp(other : self) : Int32 def lt(other : self) : Bool cmp(other) < 0 end def gt(other : self) : Bool cmp(other) > 0 end end pub trait Num : Cmp # Class-level requirements. `Enumerable#sum` and `#product` need an additive # and a multiplicative identity, and an identity belongs to the type, not to # any value of it — there is no element to ask when the collection is empty. abstract def self.zero : self abstract def self.one : self abstract def add(other : self) : self abstract def mul(other : self) : self end pub trait Hashable abstract def hash_key : Int32 end impl Cmp for Int32 def cmp(other : self) : Int32 self - other end end impl Num for Int32 def self.zero : self 0 end def self.one : self 1 end def add(other : self) : self self + other end def mul(other : self) : self self * other end end impl Hashable for Int32 def hash_key : Int32 self end end impl Cmp for String def cmp(other : self) : Int32 self <=> other end end impl Hashable for String def hash_key : Int32 size end end
files.samples/iyi/webapp.iyi: # The Sinatra feel, kept — but written by the consumer rather than injected by # the library. This is the whole argument of SPEC.md II.3 in one file. module samples/webapp import kemal/dsl import kemal/router using kemal/dsl using kemal/router::{Router, Context} before_all do |env| nil end get "/" do |env| "home" end get "/users" do |env| "all users" end post "/users" do |env| "created" end # A route may return anything implementing `IntoBody`, which is strictly more # than Kemal allows: Kemal coerces non-String results to "" at runtime. get "/count" do |env| 42 end # A route returning a type with no impl is refused where it is written: # # get "/bad" do |env| # [1, 2, 3] # end # # => Array(Int32) does not implement Kemal::Router::IntoBody, # # required by `B` in `get` # # Kemal cannot say this. `HTTP::Server::Context -> _` accepts the block and # silently returns an empty body on every request. users = Router.new users.get "/" do |env| "users index" end # The sub-router is a block parameter rather than the block's `self`: R-2 asks # an exported `def` to describe its block, and a block whose `self` changes is # the one shape no annotation can describe yet. files.site/records/break/errors_non_exhaustive: # Breaks the error rule in SPEC.md III.1: an error is an ordinary member of a # union, so handling one needs no new machinery, only the totality check a # `case` already performs. `read` can return an `IOError` and this `case` has # no branch for it, which is the same mistake as ignoring a returned error and # is caught by the same check. module diagnostics/errors_non_exhaustive pub struct IOError getter path : String def initialize(@path : String) end end # `Error` is the compiler's trait, which is what lets a union member be an # error member without any name in scope deciding it. impl Error for IOError def message : String "no such file: #{path}" end end pub def read(path : String) : String | IOError return IOError.new(path) if path == "missing" "12" end case read("missing") in String then puts it end

That restriction is # what makes a type's method set knowable from its declarations alone. module diagnostics/r3_orphan_impl import dep/greeter import dep/user using dep/greeter using dep/user impl Greet for User def greet : String "Hello, #{name}." end end puts User.new("iyi").greet
